claim: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer death and is responsible for over 50,000 deaths annually in the United States.
source: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer death and is responsible for over 50,000 deaths annually in the United States (Siegel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2019

claim: The probability of being diagnosed with CRC in one's lifetime is 1 in 24.
source: The probability of being diagnosed with CRC in one's lifetime is 1 in 24, and there are over 100,000 new cases diagnosed annually in the United States alone.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the introduction without specific citation, but presented as established knowledge

claim: There are over 100,000 new CRC cases diagnosed annually in the United States.
source: The probability of being diagnosed with CRC in one's lifetime is 1 in 24, and there are over 100,000 new cases diagnosed annually in the United States alone.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the introduction without specific citation, but presented as established knowledge

claim: The 5-year survival rate of localized CRC is 90%.
source: While the 5-year survival rate of localized and regional disease is 90 and 71%, respectively, patients with metastatic disease have just a 14% 5-year survival rate (Early detection, diagnosis, and staging, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Early detection, diagnosis, and staging, 2021

claim: The 5-year survival rate of regional CRC is 71%.
source: While the 5-year survival rate of localized and regional disease is 90 and 71%, respectively, patients with metastatic disease have just a 14% 5-year survival rate (Early detection, diagnosis, and staging, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Early detection, diagnosis, and staging, 2021

claim: Patients with metastatic CRC have a 14% 5-year survival rate.
source: While the 5-year survival rate of localized and regional disease is 90 and 71%, respectively, patients with metastatic disease have just a 14% 5-year survival rate (Early detection, diagnosis, and staging, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Early detection, diagnosis, and staging, 2021

claim: Nearly 90% of all cancer deaths is attributed to metastasis.
source: Dissemination to other organs is the cause of high mortality in most cancers as nearly 90% of all cancer deaths is attributed to metastasis (Mehlen and Puisieux, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mehlen and Puisieux, 2006

claim: The most common sites of CRC metastases include the liver, lungs, and peritoneum.
source: The most common sites of CRC metastases include the liver, lungs, and peritoneum (peritoneal carcinomatosis).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: The standard of care for CRC patients with advanced metastatic disease is commonly combination front-line chemotherapy treatment.
source: While surgery and radiation remain curative options for patients with localized disease, the standard of care for CRC patients with advanced metastatic disease is commonly combination front-line chemotherapy treatment (Werner and Heinemann, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Werner and Heinemann, 2016

claim: Fluorouracil (5-FU) and leucovorin (LV) in combination work together to inhibit DNA and RNA synthesis and modulate tumor growth.
source: These chemotherapy regimens typically include fluorouracil (5-FU) and leucovorin (LV) in combination, which work together to inhibit DNA and RNA synthesis and modulate tumor growth, extending median survival in patients from 9 months (with palliative care) to over 12 months (Rodriguez-Bigas et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodriguez-Bigas et al., 2003

claim: 5-FU/LV combination extends median survival in CRC patients from 9 months (with palliative care) to over 12 months.
source: These chemotherapy regimens typically include fluorouracil (5-FU) and leucovorin (LV) in combination, which work together to inhibit DNA and RNA synthesis and modulate tumor growth, extending median survival in patients from 9 months (with palliative care) to over 12 months (Rodriguez-Bigas et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodriguez-Bigas et al., 2003

claim: Oxaliplatin upon binding to DNA forms DNA adducts to cause irreversible transcriptional errors, resulting in cellular apoptosis.
source: Oxaliplatin is a chemotherapeutic agent that upon binding to DNA forms DNA adducts to cause irreversible transcriptional errors, resulting in cellular apoptosis.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about oxaliplatin mechanism

claim: When oxaliplatin is administered with 5-FU/LV (FOLFOX), the objective response rate is 50% in previously untreated patients.
source: When oxaliplatin is administered with 5-FU/LV (FOLFOX), the objective response rate is 50% in previously untreated patients, increasing the median overall survival to 18–24 months (Rodriguez-Bigas et al., 2003; Briffa et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rodriguez-Bigas et al., 2003 and Briffa et al., 2017

claim: FOLFOX increases the median overall survival to 18–24 months.
source: When oxaliplatin is administered with 5-FU/LV (FOLFOX), the objective response rate is 50% in previously untreated patients, increasing the median overall survival to 18–24 months (Rodriguez-Bigas et al., 2003; Briffa et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rodriguez-Bigas et al., 2003 and Briffa et al., 2017

claim: Patients who eventually succumb to CRC frequently develop chemoresistant subpopulations of cancer cells via intrinsic or acquired mechanisms.
source: While there have been incremental advances in extending survival using FOLFOX and other oxaliplatin-containing chemotherapeutics, patients who eventually succumb to the disease frequently develop chemoresistant subpopulations of cancer cells via intrinsic or acquired mechanisms (Briffa et al., 2017; Martinez-Balibrea et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Briffa et al., 2017 and Martinez-Balibrea et al., 2015

claim: Mechanisms of oxaliplatin resistance in tumors include alterations in responses to DNA damage, cell death pathways, NF-κB signaling, and cellular transport.
source: Mechanisms of oxaliplatin resistance in tumors include alterations in responses to DNA damage, cell death pathways (e.g., apoptosis, necrosis), NF-κB signaling, and cellular transport (Martinez-Balibrea et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martinez-Balibrea et al., 2015

claim: Multiple studies suggest that chemoresistant subpopulations may be increasingly susceptible to adjuvant therapies.
source: Despite the robustness of these oxaliplatin-resistant cancer cells, multiple studies suggest that chemoresistant subpopulations may be increasingly susceptible to adjuvant therapies (Martinez-Balibrea et al., 2015; Sussman et al., 2007; Jeught et al., 2018; Combès et al., 2019; Ruiz de Porras et al., 2016; Cuello et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: TRAIL is a member of the TNF family of proteins and induces apoptosis in cancer cells via binding to transmembrane death receptors.
source: Tumor necrosis factor‐related apoptosis‐inducing ligand (TRAIL) is a member of the TNF family of proteins and induces apoptosis in cancer cells via binding to transmembrane death receptors (von Karstedt et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to von Karstedt et al., 2017

claim: The binding of TRAIL to trimerized death receptor 4 (DR4) and 5 (DR5) initiates an intracellular apoptotic cascade beginning with the recruitment of death domains and formation of the death‐inducing signaling complex (DISC).
source: The binding of TRAIL to trimerized death receptor 4 (DR4) and 5 (DR5) initiates an intracellular apoptotic cascade beginning with the recruitment of death domains and formation of the death‐inducing signaling complex (DISC).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about TRAIL mechanism

claim: Lipid rafts (LRs) are microdomains in the plasma membrane lipid bilayer that are enriched in cholesterol and sphingolipids.
source: Lipid rafts (LRs) are microdomains in the plasma membrane lipid bilayer that are enriched in cholesterol and sphingolipids, with a propensity to assemble specific transmembrane and GPI-anchored proteins (Simons and Toomre, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simons and Toomre, 2000

claim: Lipid rafts play major roles in tumor progression, metastasis, and cell death.
source: Mounting evidence has demonstrated that LRs play major roles in tumor progression, metastasis, and cell death (Greenlee et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Greenlee et al., 2021

claim: Translocation into LRs can augment signaling for a variety of cancer-implicated receptors, including growth factor receptors (IGFR and EGFR) and death receptors (Fas and Death receptors 4/5).
source: Studies have shown that translocation into LRs can augment signaling for a variety of cancer-implicated receptors, including growth factor receptors (IGFR and EGFR) and death receptors (Fas and Death receptors 4/5) (Laurentiis et al., 2007; Marconi et al., 2013; Mollinedo and Gajate, 2020; George and Wu, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Translocation of death receptors into rafts enhances apoptotic signaling through the formation of clusters of apoptotic signaling molecule-enriched rafts (CASMER).
source: Translocation of death receptors into rafts enhances apoptotic signaling through the formation of clusters of apoptotic signaling molecule-enriched rafts (CASMER), which act as scaffolds to facilitate trimerization and supramolecular clustering of receptors (Mollinedo and Gajate, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mollinedo and Gajate, 2020

claim: Higher-order oligomerization of death receptors is necessary for effective apoptotic signaling in cancer cells.
source: It has become increasingly evident that higher-order oligomerization of death receptors is necessary for effective apoptotic signaling in cancer cells (Naval et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Naval et al., 2019

claim: Combination treatment of chemotherapeutic agents with TRAIL may sensitize cancer cells to TRAIL-mediated apoptosis through death receptor upregulation.
source: Studies have shown that combination treatment of chemotherapeutic agents with TRAIL may sensitize cancer cells to TRAIL-mediated apoptosis through a variety of mechanisms, including death receptor upregulation (Nagane et al., 2000; Gibson et al., 2000; Baritaki et al., 2007), suppression of apoptotic inhibitors within the intrinsic pathway (El Fajoui et al., 2011), and redistribution of death receptors into LRs (Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nagane et al., 2000; Gibson et al., 2000; Baritaki et al., 2007

claim: Combination treatment of chemotherapeutic agents with TRAIL may sensitize cancer cells to TRAIL-mediated apoptosis through suppression of apoptotic inhibitors within the intrinsic pathway.
source: Studies have shown that combination treatment of chemotherapeutic agents with TRAIL may sensitize cancer cells to TRAIL-mediated apoptosis through a variety of mechanisms, including death receptor upregulation (Nagane et al., 2000; Gibson et al., 2000; Baritaki et al., 2007), suppression of apoptotic inhibitors within the intrinsic pathway (El Fajoui et al., 2011), and redistribution of death receptors into LRs (Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to El Fajoui et al., 2011

claim: Combination treatment of chemotherapeutic agents with TRAIL may sensitize cancer cells to TRAIL-mediated apoptosis through redistribution of death receptors into LRs.
source: Studies have shown that combination treatment of chemotherapeutic agents with TRAIL may sensitize cancer cells to TRAIL-mediated apoptosis through a variety of mechanisms, including death receptor upregulation (Nagane et al., 2000; Gibson et al., 2000; Baritaki et al., 2007), suppression of apoptotic inhibitors within the intrinsic pathway (El Fajoui et al., 2011), and redistribution of death receptors into LRs (Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2009

claim: No study has examined whether surviving oxaliplatin-resistant subpopulations of cancer cells have an enhanced sensitivity to TRAIL.
source: However, no study has examined whether surviving oxaliplatin-resistant subpopulations of cancer cells have an enhanced sensitivity to TRAIL.
evidence: Stated as a gap in the literature

claim: Oxaliplatin-resistant cells show enhanced sensitivity to TRAIL-mediated apoptosis through LR translocation of DR4.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that oxaliplatin-resistant cells show enhanced sensitivity to TRAIL-mediated apoptosis through LR translocation of DR4.
evidence: Primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: Oxaliplatin-resistant HT29, SW620, and HCT116 cell lines showed increased maximum TRAIL sensitization levels compared to their parental counterparts.
source: Interestingly, oxaliplatin-resistant HT29, SW620, and HCT116 cell lines showed increased maximum TRAIL sensitization levels compared to their parental counterparts, while SW480 cells showed similar or decreased sensitization levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: SW480 cells showed similar or decreased TRAIL sensitization levels in oxaliplatin-resistant derivatives compared to parental cells.
source: Interestingly, oxaliplatin-resistant HT29, SW620, and HCT116 cell lines showed increased maximum TRAIL sensitization levels compared to their parental counterparts, while SW480 cells showed similar or decreased sensitization levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: A chemoresistant phenotype resulted in augmented TRAIL-mediated apoptosis in two cell lines based on IC50 values.
source: IC50 values demonstrate that a chemoresistant phenotype resulted in augmented TRAIL-mediated apoptosis in two cell lines (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by IC50 data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Only 33.3% of parental SW620 cells were found to be in late-stage apoptosis after 24 hr treatment with 1000 ng/ml TRAIL compared to 60.6% for OxR cells.
source: In SW620 cells, large differences in apoptosis were observed when treated with the highest concentration of TRAIL (1000 ng/ml) (Figure 1C). Only 33.3% of parental cells were found to be in late-stage apoptosis after 24 hr compared to 60.6% for OxR cells.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C

claim: SW620 OxR cells exhibited over a threefold increase in the population of JC-1 red (-) cells, indicating increased mitochondrial depolarization.
source: To determine if the observed differences in apoptosis were due to enhanced mitochondrial outer membrane permeability, a JC-1 dye was used. SW620 OxR cells exhibited over a threefold increase in the population of JC-1 red (-) cells, indicating increased mitochondrial depolarization (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by JC-1 assay data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Mitochondrial depolarization was significantly enhanced in SW620 OxR cells for TRAIL concentrations of 50 ng/ml and higher.
source: Mitochondrial depolarization was significantly enhanced in OxR cells for TRAIL concentrations of 50 ng/ml and higher (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Enhanced TRAIL-mediated apoptosis is occurring, at least in part, via the intrinsic pathway and mitochondrial disruption.
source: These results demonstrate that enhanced TRAIL-mediated apoptosis is occurring, at least in part, via the intrinsic pathway and mitochondrial disruption.
evidence: Inference based on JC-1 mitochondrial depolarization data

claim: HCT116 OxR cells showed upregulated pro-apoptotic transcripts cytochrome-c and caspase-4.
source: HCT116 OxR cells showed upregulated pro-apoptotic transcripts cytochrome-c and caspase-4 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR array data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Cytochrome-c is released from the mitochondria into the cytosol after mitochondrial permeabilization, binding to adaptor molecule apoptosis-protease activating factor 1 (Apaf-1) to form the apoptosome and initiate downstream caspase signaling.
source: Cytochrome-c is released from the mitochondria into the cytosol after mitochondrial permeabilization, binding to adaptor molecule apoptosis-protease activating factor 1 (Apaf-1) to form the apoptosome and initiate downstream caspase signaling (Garrido et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garrido et al., 2006

claim: Caspase-4 is localized to the ER and initiates apoptosis in response to ER stress.
source: Caspase-4 is localized to the ER and initiates apoptosis in response to ER stress (Hitomi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hitomi et al., 2004

claim: SW620 OxR cells had upregulated Fas, a cell surface death receptor that acts similarly in apoptotic signaling to DR4/DR5 via binding of Fas ligand.
source: Interestingly, SW620 OxR cells had upregulated Fas, a cell surface death receptor that acts similarly in apoptotic signaling to DR4/DR5 via binding of Fas ligand (Özören and El-Deiry, 2003), and osteoprotegerin, a soluble decoy receptor that sequesters TRAIL and inhibits apoptosis (Sandra et al., 2006; Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR array data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Özören and El-Deiry, 2003

claim: SW620 OxR cells had upregulated osteoprotegerin, a soluble decoy receptor that sequesters TRAIL and inhibits apoptosis.
source: Interestingly, SW620 OxR cells had upregulated Fas, a cell surface death receptor that acts similarly in apoptotic signaling to DR4/DR5 via binding of Fas ligand (Özören and El-Deiry, 2003), and osteoprotegerin, a soluble decoy receptor that sequesters TRAIL and inhibits apoptosis (Sandra et al., 2006; Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR array data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Sandra et al., 2006

claim: Upregulated Fas expression in SW620 OxR cells was confirmed via surface staining and flow cytometry.
source: Upregulated Fas expression in SW620 OxR cells was confirmed via surface staining and flow cytometry; however, receptor neutralization with the ZB4 anti-Fas antibody had no effect on TRAIL sensitization when treated in combination with TRAIL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: Receptor neutralization with the ZB4 anti-Fas antibody had no effect on TRAIL sensitization when treated in combination with TRAIL.
source: Upregulated Fas expression in SW620 OxR cells was confirmed via surface staining and flow cytometry; however, receptor neutralization with the ZB4 anti-Fas antibody had no effect on TRAIL sensitization when treated in combination with TRAIL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: Both HCT116 and SW620 OxR cell lines had caspase-10 as the most significantly downregulated transcript.
source: Notably, both HCT116 and SW620 OxR cell lines had caspase-10 as the most significantly downregulated transcript.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR array data shown in Figure 2A and 2B

claim: Knock-out efficiency of caspase-10 in SW620 cells was found to be 93%.
source: To determine whether this was of consequence to the observed TRAIL sensitization, an SW620 caspase-10 knockout cell line was created using a multi-guide sgRNA CRISPR-Cas9 approach. Knock-out (KO) efficiency was found to be 93% (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Caspase-10 KO cells showed only a slight decrease in cell viability after 24 hr of TRAIL treatment.
source: Caspase-10 KO cells showed only a slight decrease in cell viability after 24 hr of TRAIL treatment (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The number of late-stage apoptotic cells remained similar between caspase-10 KO and control cell lines.
source: The number of late-stage apoptotic cells remained similar between cell lines (Figure 2E), and the maximum TRAIL sensitization observed was insignificant following caspase-10 KO (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The maximum TRAIL sensitization observed was insignificant following caspase-10 KO.
source: The number of late-stage apoptotic cells remained similar between cell lines (Figure 2E), and the maximum TRAIL sensitization observed was insignificant following caspase-10 KO (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Oxaliplatin-resistant cells have increased DR4 in both HCT116 and SW620 cell lines as shown by confocal microscopy.
source: Confocal microscopy showed that oxaliplatin-resistant cells have increased DR4 in both HCT116 (Figure 3A) and SW620 (Figure 3B) cell lines.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: OxR derivative cell lines had significantly increased DR4 area per cell.
source: To quantify receptor expression, total DR4 area per cell was analyzed for at least 70 cells. Analysis showed OxR derivative cell lines had significantly increased DR4 area per cell (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C

claim: There were no differences in cell size between parental and OxR derivatives for all four cell lines.
source: There were no differences in cell size between parental and OxR derivatives for all four cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Both HCT116 OxR and SW620 OxR cells showed significant increases in DR4 surface expression.
source: Flow cytometry staining of non-permeabilized cells was used to determine if this death receptor increase was also observed on the cell surface. Both HCT116 OxR and SW620 OxR cells showed significant increases in DR4 surface expression (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Total and surface DR4 expression was similar between parental and OxR derivatives in mildly sensitized HT29 cells and unsensitized SW480 cells.
source: Total and surface DR4 expression was similar between parental and OxR derivatives in mildly sensitized HT29 cells and unsensitized SW480 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: Increases in DR4 expression of OxR derivatives were confirmed via western blot but were only significant in SW620 cells.
source: Increases in DR4 expression of OxR derivatives were also confirmed via western blot but were only significant in SW620 cells (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E and 3F

claim: OxR HCT116, SW620, and HT29 cells all displayed increases in DR5 area per cell.
source: OxR HCT116, SW620, and HT29 cells all displayed increases in DR5 area per cell, while SW480 OxR cells had significant decreases in total DR5 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–D

claim: SW480 OxR cells had significant decreases in total DR5 expression.
source: OxR HCT116, SW620, and HT29 cells all displayed increases in DR5 area per cell, while SW480 OxR cells had significant decreases in total DR5 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–D

claim: Total receptor area per cell was considerably lower for DR5 compared to DR4.
source: However, total receptor area per cell was considerably lower for DR5 compared to DR4.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of DR4 and DR5 quantification data

claim: Expression of surface DR5 was only significantly upregulated in SW620 OxR cells.
source: Additionally, expression of surface DR5, analyzed via flow cytometry, was only significantly upregulated in SW620 OxR cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4E

claim: Western blot data show no change in DR5 expression in HCT116 OxR cells.
source: This is further confounded by western blot data, which show no change in DR5 expression in HCT116 OxR cells, and a significant decrease in SW620 OxR cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A, B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A, B

claim: Western blot data show a significant decrease in DR5 expression in SW620 OxR cells.
source: This is further confounded by western blot data, which show no change in DR5 expression in HCT116 OxR cells, and a significant decrease in SW620 OxR cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A, B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A, B

claim: All cell lines exhibited no meaningful difference in surface DcR1 and DcR2 expression between parental and OxR derivatives.
source: While some studies have shown that chemotherapy-induced changes in TRAIL sensitivity have been linked to modulation or augmentation of decoy receptors (Toscano et al., 2008), all cell lines exhibited no meaningful difference in surface DcR1 and DcR2 expression between parental and OxR derivatives (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6

claim: SW620 OxR cells exhibited significant increases in the number of apoptotic cells after 24 hr of mapatumumab treatment, including a threefold increase in apoptosis at concentrations of 10 µg/ml.
source: Given the consistency in data suggesting DR4 upregulation in TRAIL-sensitized OxR cell lines, cells were treated with the DR4-agonist monoclonal antibody mapatumumab to determine DR4 specificity. SW620 OxR cells exhibited significant increases in the number of apoptotic cells after 24 hr of treatment, including a threefold increase in apoptosis at concentrations of 10 µg/ml (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Cell viability of SW620 cells closely paralleled TRAIL treatments: parental cells remained resistant at high doses while OxR cells exhibited a dose-responsive decrease in cell viability.
source: Cell viability closely paralleled TRAIL treatments: parental cells remained resistant at high doses while OxR cells exhibited a dose-responsive decrease in cell viability (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3H

claim: The maximum mapatumumab sensitization was calculated to be greater than 40% for oxaliplatin-resistant HCT116 and SW620 cells.
source: The maximum mapatumumab sensitization was calculated to be greater than 40% for oxaliplatin-resistant HCT116 and SW620 cells (Figure 3I), providing more causal evidence for a DR4-associated mechanism.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3I

claim: OxR phenotypes had enhanced DR4 translocation into LRs in HCT116 and SW620 cells.
source: Binary projections of colocalization events between DR4 and LRs demonstrate that OxR phenotypes had enhanced DR4 translocation into LRs in HCT116 and SW620 cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 4A

claim: HCT116 OxR and SW620 OxR cells have significantly enhanced DR4 localized into LRs, each with an over fourfold increase.
source: Quantification of total area of colocalization events showed that HCT116 OxR and SW620 OxR cells have significantly enhanced DR4 localized into LRs, each with an over fourfold increase (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The areas of DR4/LR colocalized events per cell were not significantly different in HT29 and SW480 cells.
source: The areas of DR4/LR colocalized events per cell were not significantly different in HT29 and SW480 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D

claim: The Manders' overlap was significantly greater in OxR cells in HCT116 and SW620 cell lines.
source: Other methods of colocalization analysis, including calculation of the Manders' Correlation Coefficient (MCC), supported these results, specifically in HCT116 and SW620 cell lines where the Manders' overlap was significantly greater in OxR cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by MCC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The fold change in DR4/LR colocalization area between OxR and parental cells exhibited a strong linear correlation (0.86) with TRAIL sensitization.
source: The fold change in DR4/LR colocalization area between OxR and parental cells exhibited a strong linear correlation (0.86) with TRAIL sensitization (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Colocalization of LRs with DR5 was significantly enhanced only in HCT116 and HT29 cells.
source: Colocalization of LRs with DR5 was significantly enhanced only in HCT116 and HT29 cells, and analysis of the correlation between DR5 colocalization and TRAIL sensitization resulted in a weaker correlation of 0.48 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: Analysis of the correlation between DR5 colocalization and TRAIL sensitization resulted in a weaker correlation of 0.48.
source: Colocalization of LRs with DR5 was significantly enhanced only in HCT116 and HT29 cells, and analysis of the correlation between DR5 colocalization and TRAIL sensitization resulted in a weaker correlation of 0.48 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: Quantification of LR area per cell revealed insignificant changes between parental and OxR derivatives in all cell lines except for HT29 cells, where parental cells showed significantly more rafts.
source: Quantification of LR area per cell revealed insignificant changes between parental and OxR derivatives in all cell lines except for HT29 cells, where parental cells showed significantly more rafts (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Isolated LR fractions exhibited significant increases in DR4 for both HCT116 OxR and SW620 OxR cells.
source: To confirm DR4 redistribution into rafts, western blots for DR4 were run on plasma membrane-derived LR fractions, isolated using non-ionic detergent and centrifugation. Isolated LR fractions exhibited significant increases in DR4 for both HCT116 OxR and SW620 OxR cells (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D and 4E

claim: There were no detectable levels of DR5 in western blots from LR isolated fractions.
source: There were no detectable levels of DR5 in western blots from LR isolated fractions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D

claim: Studies in hematological cancers demonstrate raft localization of DR4 but not DR5.
source: This is consistent with studies in hematological cancers that demonstrate raft localization of DR4 but not DR5 (Marconi et al., 2013; Xiao et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marconi et al., 2013 and Xiao et al., 2011

claim: Both HCT116 and SW620 OxR cells had significantly increased FRET efficiencies compared to their parental counterparts, with an over twofold and fivefold increase, respectively.
source: To further examine the proximity of DR4 and LRs between phenotypes, Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) efficiency was measured using a previously described flow cytometry protocol and calculated via a donor quenching method (Ujlaky-Nagy et al., 2018). Both HCT116 and SW620 OxR cells had significantly increased FRET efficiencies compared to their parental counterparts, with an over twofold and fivefold increase, respectively (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by FRET data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Nystatin inhibited TRAIL-mediated apoptosis in SW620 OxR cells, significantly decreasing the maximum TRAIL sensitization from 45% to 23%.
source: To probe the effects of LR modulation on DR4 clustering and TRAIL sensitization, SW620 OxR and HCT116 OxR cells were treated with 5 µM of nystatin, a cholesterol-sequestering agent that inhibits LR formation, in combination with TRAIL for 24 hr (Figure 5A, G). Nystatin inhibited TRAIL-mediated apoptosis in SW620 OxR cells, significantly decreasing the maximum TRAIL sensitization from 45% to 23% (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A, 5B, and 5G

claim: Nystatin treatment decreased DR4/LR colocalization by over 20-fold in SW620 OxR cells.
source: Nystatin treatment was found to decrease DR4/LR colocalization by over 20-fold (Figure 5C, M).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5C and 5M

claim: Nystatin treatment decreased TRAIL sensitization in HCT116 OxR cells from 62% to 1%.
source: Similar results were found in HCT116 OxR cells as nystatin treatment decreased TRAIL sensitization from 62% to 1% (Figure 5H) and decreased DR4/LR colocalization by over ninefold (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5H and 5I

claim: Nystatin treatment decreased DR4/LR colocalization by over ninefold in HCT116 OxR cells.
source: Similar results were found in HCT116 OxR cells as nystatin treatment decreased TRAIL sensitization from 62% to 1% (Figure 5H) and decreased DR4/LR colocalization by over ninefold (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5H and 5I

claim: Resveratrol has been shown to stabilize liquid-ordered domains in the plasma membrane and promote cholesterol/sphingolipid-enriched LRs.
source: To demonstrate that enhancing LR formation would have pro-apoptotic effects, parental cells were treated with 70 μM of resveratrol in combination with TRAIL for 24 hr (Figure 5D, J). Resveratrol has been shown to stabilize liquid-ordered domains in the plasma membrane and promote cholesterol/sphingolipid-enriched LRs (Neves et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neves et al., 2016

claim: Resveratrol significantly sensitized parental SW620 cells to TRAIL irrespective of TRAIL concentration with a maximum TRAIL sensitization of 68%.
source: Resveratrol significantly sensitized parental SW620 cells to TRAIL irrespective of TRAIL concentration with a maximum TRAIL sensitization of 68% (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Treatment with resveratrol coincided with significant augmentation of DR4/LR colocalization area in SW620 parental cells, an increase of over sixfold.
source: Treatment with resveratrol coincided with significant augmentation of DR4/LR colocalization area, an increase of over sixfold (Figure 5F, N).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5F and 5N

claim: Parental HCT116 cells treated with resveratrol were sensitized 59%.
source: Similarly, parental HCT116 cells treated with resveratrol were sensitized 59% (Figure 5K), corresponding with a nearly sevenfold increase in DR4/LR colocalization area per cell (Figure 5L).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5K

claim: Resveratrol treatment in HCT116 parental cells corresponded with a nearly sevenfold increase in DR4/LR colocalization area per cell.
source: Similarly, parental HCT116 cells treated with resveratrol were sensitized 59% (Figure 5K), corresponding with a nearly sevenfold increase in DR4/LR colocalization area per cell (Figure 5L).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5L

claim: DR4 has four distinct palmitoylated sites, the degree of which was enhanced in the oxaliplatin-resistant phenotype.
source: S-Palmitoylation of DR4 in SW620 parental and OxR cells was analyzed via protein precipitation, free thiol blocking, thioester cleavage of palmitate linkages, and exchange with a mass tag label to quantify the degree of palmitoylated protein. We discovered that DR4 has four distinct palmitoylated sites, the degree of which was enhanced in the oxaliplatin-resistant phenotype (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by palmitoylation assay data shown in Figure 6A

claim: OxR cells had a significantly higher percentage of DR4 that was palmitoylated (55% compared to 43%).
source: Quantifying the percentage of palmitoylated protein in relation to input fraction (IFC) and non-mass tag preserved controls (APC-) validated that OxR cells had a significantly higher percentage of DR4 that was palmitoylated (55% compared to 43%) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Total cellular palmitoylation was unchanged between parental and OxR cells.
source: To determine whether enhanced palmitoylation was specific to DR4 and not a ubiquitous characteristic of the OxR phenotype, total cellular protein palmitoylation was measured and analyzed via flow cytometry (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). Fluorescent azide labeling of palmitic acid confirmed that total cellular palmitoylation was unchanged between parental and OxR cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and 1B

claim: Treating SW620 OxR cells with 3.5 μM 2BP in combination with TRAIL significantly reduced TRAIL sensitization and increased the IC50 to over 1000 ng/ml.
source: To further examine the relationship between DR4 palmitoylation and TRAIL sensitization in OxR cells, the irreversible palmitoylation inhibitor 2-bromopalmitate (2BP) was used. 2BP is a commonly used palmitate analog that is thought to bind to palmitoyl acyl transferase, forming an inhibitory enzyme complex (Draper and Smith, 2009). Treating SW620 OxR cells with 3.5 μM 2BP in combination with TRAIL significantly reduced TRAIL sensitization and increased the IC50 to over 1000 ng/ml (Figure 6C, E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6C and 6E

claim: 2BP significantly reduced the number of apoptotic cells in both parental and OxR cells.
source: 2BP significantly reduced the number of apoptotic cells in both parental and OxR cells, demonstrating the importance of DR4 palmitoylation in TRAIL signaling, particularly in chemoresistant cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6D

claim: TRAIL liposomes significantly decreased the average percentage of viable CTCs in patient blood to 43% compared to just 86% when treated with oxaliplatin.
source: Blood samples were treated with TRAIL liposomes or control treatments under hematogenous circulatory shear conditions in a cone-and-plate viscometer. TRAIL liposomes significantly decreased the average percentage of viable CTCs in patient blood to 43% compared to just 86% when treated with oxaliplatin (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7B

claim: TRAIL liposomal therapy reduced total viable CTC counts by 58% compared to control liposomes.
source: TRAIL liposomal therapy reduced total viable CTC counts by 58% compared to control liposomes, and over 32% compared to oxaliplatin after just 4 hr in circulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: TRAIL liposomal therapy reduced total viable CTC counts by over 32% compared to oxaliplatin after just 4 hr in circulation.
source: TRAIL liposomal therapy reduced total viable CTC counts by 58% compared to control liposomes, and over 32% compared to oxaliplatin after just 4 hr in circulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: In two patients (P10 and P11), there were no detectable viable CTCs in blood samples treated with TRAIL liposomes.
source: Notably, in two patients (P10 and P11), there were no detectable viable CTCs in blood samples treated with TRAIL liposomes.
evidence: Stated as an observation from patient data

claim: Patients that presented with metastases in the liver or bone showed a greater reduction in viable CTCs (69 and 71%, respectively) than patients with both lung and liver metastases (32%).
source: When categorizing patients by location of metastasis, patients that presented with metastases in the liver or bone showed a greater reduction in viable CTCs (69 and 71%, respectively) than patients with both lung and liver metastases (32%) (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Patients undergoing FOLFOX or capecitabine + oxaliplatin had the highest reduction in CTCs (65 and 60%, respectively).
source: Patients had similar CTC reductions regardless of their treatment at the time of blood draw, while those undergoing FOLFOX or capecitabine + oxaliplatin had the highest reduction in CTCs (65 and 60%, respectively) (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7E

claim: There was no significant difference in CTC response to TRAIL liposomes when categorizing patients as either oxaliplatin-sensitive or -resistant.
source: When categorizing patients as either oxaliplatin-sensitive or -resistant, based on their response to 5 μM oxaliplatin under hematogenous circulatory-shear conditions (threshold 80% CTC viability), there was no significant difference in CTC response to TRAIL liposomes (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A

claim: There was no significant difference in reduction of viable CTCs from the administration of liposomal TRAIL when grouping patients by those undergoing oxaliplatin chemotherapy and those who had failed oxaliplatin previously.
source: Likewise, grouping patients by those undergoing oxaliplatin chemotherapy and those who had failed oxaliplatin previously, there was no significant difference in reduction of viable CTCs from the administration of liposomal TRAIL (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B

claim: Decreasing LR colocalization with DR4 coincided with reduced efficacy of TRAIL liposomes (higher percentage of viable CTCs after treatment), with a negative slope that significantly deviated from zero.
source: Patient CTCs were also stained for DR4 and LRs to examine the relationships between raft colocalization, treatment efficacy, and oxaliplatin resistance. Decreasing LR colocalization with DR4 coincided with reduced efficacy of TRAIL liposomes (higher percentage of viable CTCs after treatment), with a negative slope that significantly deviated from zero (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7F

claim: Increasing LR DR4 corresponded with increasing resistance to oxaliplatin (higher percentage of viable CTCs after oxaliplatin treatment), with a positive slope that significantly deviated from zero.
source: Additionally, increasing LR DR4 corresponded with increasing resistance to oxaliplatin (higher percentage of viable CTCs after oxaliplatin treatment), with a positive slope that significantly deviated from zero (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7G

claim: Patient 7 exhibited increased DR4/LR colocalization in CTCs despite progression while on FOLFOX treatment.
source: Patient 7 was undergoing the first cycle of FOLFOX at the time of draw 1 and progressed while on FOLFOX for draws 2 and 3. However, DR4 and LR staining of CTCs revealed increased DR4/LR colocalization despite progression (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 7H

claim: This is the first study to investigate the role of lipid rafts in primary CTCs.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first study investigating LR/protein interactions in primary CTCs (Greenlee et al., 2021).
evidence: Stated as a novel contribution of the study

claim: Palmitoylation of DR4 has proven to be critical for receptor oligomerization and LR translocation, both obligatory for effective TRAIL-mediated apoptotic signaling.
source: Palmitoylation is the reversible, post-translational addition of the saturated fatty acid palmitate to the cystine residue of proteins. Palmitoylation of DR4 has proven to be critical for receptor oligomerization and LR translocation, both obligatory for effective TRAIL-mediated apoptotic signaling (Rossin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rossin et al., 2009

claim: Both Fas receptor and DR4 are palmitoylated, while DR5 is not.
source: There is evidence that both Fas receptor and DR4 are palmitoylated, while DR5 is not (Rossin et al., 2009; Chakrabandhu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rossin et al., 2009 and Chakrabandhu et al., 2007

claim: Palmitoylation of δ-catenin in dorsal root ganglion was significantly increased after chronic oxaliplatin treatment in rats.
source: Interestingly, in a sensory neuron study in rats, palmitoylation of δ-catenin in dorsal root ganglion was significantly increased after chronic oxaliplatin treatment (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018

claim: Oxaliplatin-resistant cell lines were previously derived from exposure to increasing concentrations of oxaliplatin until a 10-fold increase in IC50 was achieved.
source: Briefly, oxaliplatin-resistant cell lines were previously derived from exposure to increasing concentrations of oxaliplatin until a 10-fold increase in IC50 was achieved (Dallas et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2006; Tanaka et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dallas et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2006; Tanaka et al., 2015

claim: Oxaliplatin-resistant cells were found to have increased invasion and motility compared to parental cells.
source: Moreover, oxaliplatin-resistant cells were found to have increased invasion and motility compared to parental cells, consistent with literature reporting their derivation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Transwell assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Blood samples from metastatic CRC patients were treated with TRAIL liposomes, and a 57% reduction of viable circulating tumor cells (CTCs) was observed.
source: Blood samples from metastatic CRC patients were treated with TRAIL liposomes, and a 57% reduction of viable circulating tumor cells (CTCs) was observed.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding

claim: Increased DR4/lipid raft colocalization in CTCs was found to correspond with increased oxaliplatin resistance and increased efficacy of TRAIL liposomes.
source: Increased DR4/lipid raft colocalization in CTCs was found to correspond with increased oxaliplatin resistance and increased efficacy of TRAIL liposomes.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding, supported by data in Figure 7F and 7G

claim: Oxaliplatin-resistant CRC cells are sensitized to TRAIL-mediated apoptosis.
source: We demonstrate that oxaliplatin-resistant CRC cells are sensitized to TRAIL-mediated apoptosis.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding

claim: Oxaliplatin-resistant cells exhibited transcriptional downregulation of caspase-10.
source: Oxaliplatin-resistant cells exhibited transcriptional downregulation of caspase-10, but this had minimal effects on TRAIL sensitivity following CRISPR-Cas9 deletion of caspase-10 in parental cells.
evidence: Stated in the abstract, supported by RT-PCR and CRISPR data in Figure 2

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 deletion of caspase-10 in parental cells had minimal effects on TRAIL sensitivity.
source: Oxaliplatin-resistant cells exhibited transcriptional downregulation of caspase-10, but this had minimal effects on TRAIL sensitivity following CRISPR-Cas9 deletion of caspase-10 in parental cells.
evidence: Stated in the abstract, supported by CRISPR data in Figure 2D-F

claim: Sensitization effects in oxaliplatin-resistant cells were found to be a result of increased DR4.
source: Sensitization effects in oxaliplatin-resistant cells were found to be a result of increased DR4, as well as significantly enhanced DR4 palmitoylation and translocation into lipid rafts.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding, supported by data in Figures 3 and 4

claim: Sensitization effects in oxaliplatin-resistant cells were found to be a result of significantly enhanced DR4 palmitoylation.
source: Sensitization effects in oxaliplatin-resistant cells were found to be a result of increased DR4, as well as significantly enhanced DR4 palmitoylation and translocation into lipid rafts.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding, supported by palmitoylation data in Figure 6

claim: Sensitization effects in oxaliplatin-resistant cells were found to be a result of significantly enhanced DR4 translocation into lipid rafts.
source: Sensitization effects in oxaliplatin-resistant cells were found to be a result of increased DR4, as well as significantly enhanced DR4 palmitoylation and translocation into lipid rafts.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding, supported by colocalization data in Figure 4

claim: Raft perturbation via nystatin and resveratrol significantly altered DR4/raft colocalization and TRAIL sensitivity.
source: Raft perturbation via nystatin and resveratrol significantly altered DR4/raft colocalization and TRAIL sensitivity.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding, supported by data in Figure 5
